facts.fact: Healthcare managers interviewed for the study (15 managers, ||Kharas region and national level) state that district HIS officers key the monthly paper summary forms sent in by health facilities into the DHIS2 aggregate module at the district office; the document gives no date for this, so the published date is used.

The managers state that DHIS2 is used at district, regional and national levels while primary health facilities still report on paper tools, and the authors add that most facilities continue to rely on paper and that DHIS2 at the point of care is slow to arrive; no count or share is given, and no date, so the published date is used.

Managers state that DHIS2 is managed centrally by the Ministry of Health and Social Services, on a central server at headquarters where national staff alone change the design, add indicators and run backups; no date is given, so the published date is used.

Managers state that external donors provide the money and technical expertise for customising DHIS2, fund training and buy the computers and other equipment, and one calls the reliance on outsourced expertise costly and unsustainable; no domestic budget line is mentioned and no date is given, so the published date is used.

Managers state that Namibia has no specific policy on health information systems, that an HIS strategy exists only as an unpromulgated draft, and that the one official guiding document (the HIS2K reference manual) is outdated; no date is given, so the published date is used.

Managers state that the Ministry of Health and Social Services has developed an e-Health Strategy (cited in the references as the National eHealth Strategy 2021-2025) to guide a digital platform for capturing patient data, starting with a billing module on pilot at Katutura and Windhoek Central hospitals; no date is given for the pilot, so the published date is used.
